title: Spike-Triggered Closed-Loop Auditory Stimulation in Epilepsy Patients
author: Ngo, Born, et al.

steps.title: Welcome participants and ensure comfort
steps.instruction: Allocate approximately 1.5 h for pre‑sleep procedures. Participants arrive at the laboratory in the evening, about two hours before their usual bedtime. For pediatric patients, ensure at least one parent is present, quickly establish a trusting relationship, allow the child to bring a favorite stuffed animal or toy, and arrange for the parent to sleep in a room adjacent to the laboratory or on a second bed inside the laboratory.

steps.title: Screen hearing ability
steps.instruction: Conduct pure‑tone audiograms at 500, 1000, 2000, and 4000 Hz to detect undiagnosed hearing impairments. Exclude any participant whose pure‑tone average (PTA) exceeds 30 dB.

steps.title: Apply EEG electrodes and headphones
steps.instruction: Place the required EEG electrodes and fit in‑ear headphones. Secure the headphones with medical tape over the ears and along the cable as needed. Use audio playback or active conversation to keep the child comfortable during the setup.

steps.title: Determine individual auditory threshold
steps.instruction: Present the stimulation tone (burst of pink noise, 50 ms duration with 5 ms rise/fall) via the headphones. Start at an inaudible level and increase the volume stepwise until the child signals perception; repeat to verify the threshold. For later stimulation, increase the volume by an additional +12 dB. Ensure the wakefulness threshold does not exceed 60 dB SPL.

steps.title: Begin sleep recording
steps.instruction: After threshold determination, send the patient (and parent, if present) to the bed to start the overnight sleep recording.

steps.title: Remove equipment after sleep
steps.instruction: Allocate 0.5–1 h for post‑sleep procedures. In the morning, once the participant is awake, remove all EEG electrodes.

steps.title: Debrief participant
steps.instruction: Conduct a debriefing conversation and fill out the debriefing questionnaire together with the child, allowing free discussion and ensuring the child feels valued.

steps.title: Offline spike detection pipeline
steps.instruction: Run offline spike detection on the recorded EEG: (a) perform fastICA decomposition and discard components lacking spike‑like waveforms; (b) back‑project the remaining components into EEG space; (c) high‑pass filter the detection electrode at 5 Hz; (d) compute the Hilbert envelope and smooth it with a moving‑average window of 50 ms; (e) set the spike detection threshold to the mean envelope plus 2.5 × standard deviation; (f) register a spike when the envelope exceeds this threshold for more than 10 ms and less than 500 ms; (g) merge putative events occurring within 50 ms of each other.

steps.title: Statistical analysis of spikes
steps.instruction: Analyze spike rates and amplitudes: pool data across participants per 30‑s stimulation block and compare conditions; also average within each participant and condition for between‑subject comparisons. Consider Bayesian multi‑layer models that incorporate within‑subject and between‑subject variance. Run simulations beforehand to verify that the number of stimulation blocks provides sufficient power for the chosen analysis.

description: The following protocol has been implemented by Klinzing et al. (2021) in patients with benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (BECTS). In this study, stimulation led to a reduction in the rate and amplitude of interictal spiking activity. Further analyses suggested this effect may result from acoustically induced activity in the thalamocortical system. There is reason to hypothesize the protocol’s applicability for other sleep epilepsies, such as continuous spike and wave during sleep (CSWS), particularly if an association with sleep spindles or, more generally, an involvement of the thalamocortical system has been demonstrated. While BECTS patients are typically between 6 and 12 years old, expanding the scope of the technique to other conditions may result in the inclusion of vastly different age groups. The method of detecting neuronal events and applying closed-loop stimulation has various conceivable applications outside the realm of epilepsy, which will not be discussed here. We will not describe general questions of obtaining ethics approval, details on informing participants, or participant reimbursement.Note: The protocol described here only considers the assessment of electrophysiological measures and was developed based on stimulation during a single night. To gauge the clinical relevance of the suppression effect, future studies could incorporate cognitive assessments of before/after or stimulation/sham differences and examine long-term effects of stimulation applied over several consecutive nights. In case the participants are pediatric patients, as in the case of BECTS, they should be accompanied by at least one parent. There may be situations during the experimental night, in which the child gets impatient, reluctant, or maybe even a bit scared. It is therefore helpful to quickly establish a trusting relationship with child and parent. Allowing the patient to bring their favorite stuffed animal or toy can make the laboratory bed feel less unknown.
